findings.body:
`unsubscribe` fetches the TopicUser record with `TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` and immediately calls `tu.notification_level` / `tu.save!` on the result without a nil check. `find_by` returns `nil` whenever the logged-in user has no `topic_users` row for that topic (e.g. they never visited or interacted with it - which is common for anyone who is not the original notification recipient, or for the recipient in edge cases where the row hasn't been created). This raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil:NilClass` and produces a 500 for a route that is publicly reachable to any authenticated user (`t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe`). Every other place in this codebase that needs a possibly-missing TopicUser row uses the upsert helper `TopicUser.change(user_id, topic_id, attrs)` (see `set_notifications` in the same controller, and `toggle_mute`) specifically to avoid this. This new action bypasses that established pattern.

Repro: log in as any user, GET `/t/<slug>/<topic_id>/unsubscribe` for a topic that user has never viewed/tracked -> 500.
findings.title: NoMethodError when no TopicUser row exists for the current user/topic

findings.body: The new `unsubscribe` action mutates `TopicUser#notification_level` (muting/downgrading the subscription) as a side effect of a plain GET request, with no confirmation step. Every other notification-state mutation in this controller (`mute`, `unmute`, `set_notifications`) is exposed via PUT (see config/routes.rb `put "t/:topic_id/mute"` etc.), which is protected by Rails' CSRF token and is not treated as safe/cacheable by intermediaries. This new endpoint is a GET, so: (1) Rails' default CSRF protection does not cover it, making it triggerable cross-site (e.g. `` on a third-party page while the target is logged in); and (2) it is exactly the class of URL (an email 'unsubscribe' link) that corporate email gateways / antivirus / link-prefetchers (Outlook Safe Links, Proofpoint, Mimecast, etc.) routinely GET automatically to scan for malware, which would silently mute the topic for the user without them ever clicking anything.
findings.title: State-changing mutation performed on a bare GET request

findings.body: The new controller defines `stopNotificiationsText` (missing an 'a' - should be `stopNotificationsText`) and the template references the same misspelled name, so it still works today, but the typo will confuse future maintainers and any code that tries to reference the correctly-spelled property (e.g. from another controller/view) will silently get `undefined` instead of an error.
findings.title: Typo in Ember controller/computed property name

findings.body: `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` (app/controllers/topics_controller.rb:105) can return nil, and the code immediately calls `tu.notification_level` unconditionally, raising `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil:NilClass`. Trivially reproducible: any logged-in user GETting `/t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` for a topic they've never visited/tracked (no `topic_users` row) crashes the request. It's also hit via the real email flow: a user who is only @mentioned/quoted/linked (never visited the topic) can lack a TopicUser row — `PostAlerter#create_notification` (app/services/post_alerter.rb:105) explicitly guards this with `.try(:notification_level)` for exactly this reason, and `send_notification_email` (app/mailers/user_notifications.rb:295) now puts this unsubscribe link in every notification email including those. No spec exercises `TopicsController#unsubscribe`. Fix direction: use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)`, the existing upsert helper used by every other write path, instead of `find_by` + `save!`.
findings.title: [P1] Unsubscribe action 500s (NoMethodError) when no TopicUser row exists for the current user/topic

findings.body: The action mutates `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly (app/controllers/topics_controller.rb:107-113) instead of going through `TopicUser.change` (app/models/topic_user.rb:77-118), which every other write path uses (`set_notifications`, `toggle_mute`, pin/unpin, bulk actions). `TopicUser.change` stamps `notifications_reason_id` whenever `notification_level` is set (topic_user.rb:87-90); the direct-write path skips this, so `notifications_reason_id` stays whatever it was before (often nil for a topic the user never explicitly acted on). `TopicUser.auto_track` (topic_user.rb:37-49), which `PostCreator` calls on every new post in a topic (`TopicUser.auto_track(user.id, topic.id, :created_post)`), only fires `if TopicUser.where(..., notifications_reason_id: nil).exists?` and force-upgrades the level back to `:tracking`. Concrete path: a user unsubscribes from a topic they hadn't explicitly configured notifications for, then later posts a reply in that same topic — their unsubscribe choice is silently discarded. This also means the action never emits the `MessageBus.publish("/topic/#{topic_id}", {notification_level_change: ...})` broadcast that keeps other open tabs/sessions in sync in real time.
findings.title: [P1] Unsubscribing is silently reverted the next time the user posts in the topic

findings.body: `:unsubscribe` was added to the `ensure_logged_in` before_filter list (topics_controller.rb:27-28), so a user opening this link from their email in a context without an active forum session (different browser/device, mobile mail app opening an external browser, cleared cookies) hits a login wall instead of unsubscribing — arguably the primary way this link gets used. This is inconsistent with the codebase's existing digest-email unsubscribe flow, `EmailController#unsubscribe`, which intentionally requires no login by authenticating via a signed, unguessable `DigestUnsubscribeKey` token instead of the session.
findings.title: [P2] Unsubscribe link requires an active login session, undermining the email-click use case

findings.body: The new routes are `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` / `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` (config/routes.rb:440-441), but every other action mutating TopicUser notification state in this controller (`mute`, `unmute`, `set_notifications`, `bookmark`) uses `put`/`post` specifically so Rails' `protect_from_forgery` (application_controller.rb:21) applies — CSRF verification only covers unsafe verbs, GET is always exempt. Because `:unsubscribe` is session-authenticated, any third-party page can trigger this mutation for a logged-in visitor via a plain `` or link, silently changing their topic notification level with no confirmation.
findings.title: [P2] Unsubscribe is a state-mutating GET with no CSRF protection, unlike every sibling notification action

findings.body: For users whose level is above `:regular` (watching/tracking), the toggle (topics_controller.rb:107-111) only steps them down to `:regular`, not `:muted`. The email copy (config/locales/server.en.yml `unsubscribe_link`) and the in-app copy (config/locales/client.en.yml `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications`: "You will stop receiving notifications for {{title}}") both promise notifications stop, but `PostAlerter#create_notification` (app/services/post_alerter.rb:105) only suppresses notification creation when the level is exactly `:muted` — a `:regular` user still gets notified on mentions/quotes/replies/links in that topic. A second click is required to actually silence it, contradicting the copy shown on the first click.
findings.title: [P2] First click doesn't fulfill the promised "stop receiving notifications" for watching/tracking users

findings.body: `routes/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6:5,14` calls `this.store.createRecord("topic", {id: params.id})`, which hydrates through the shared Ember Data-style identity map (`models/store.js.es6` `_hydrate`). If the topic is already cached in the running SPA session (e.g. the user reaches `/unsubscribe` via an in-app transition rather than a fresh page load from the email link), `afterModel`'s `topic.set("details.notificationReasonText", null)` mutates the shared `Topic`/`TopicDetails` instance in place. Because `notificationReasonText` is a getter-only computed property with zero-arity, Ember's `.set()` de-computes it into a plain `null` value permanently, so navigating back to the real topic page afterward silently and permanently loses the notification-reason tooltip for that topic instance until a full reload. Low likelihood given the primary entry point is a fresh page load from an email link, but real for in-app navigation/SPA route reuse.
findings.title: [P3] Unsubscribe route mutates the shared cached Topic instance when reached via in-app navigation

findings.body:
`unsubscribe` does:
```ruby
tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])
if tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]
```
There is no nil guard on `tu`. `TopicUser.find_by` returns nil whenever no row exists for that user/topic pair, which happens whenever the account clicking the emailed link never had `TopicUser.change` called for it (e.g. the link is opened by a different logged-in account than the recipient, or the row was otherwise never created) - `tu.notification_level` then raises `NoMethodError` on nil.

Separately, even when `tu` exists, `notification_level` is a nullable column - the pre-existing `tracking` scope explicitly does `COALESCE(topic_users.notification_level, :regular)` because rows created via `TopicUser.track_visit!` (topic_user.rb) never set `notification_level`. So `tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]` can also raise `NoMethodError: undefined method '>' for nil:NilClass` for a perfectly real, existing row.

Every other write path to `notification_level` in this codebase goes through `TopicUser.change`, which creates the row if missing and treats a nil level correctly. This new action reimplements that logic manually and drops the safety net.
findings.title: TopicsController#unsubscribe can raise NoMethodError (500) instead of handling missing/blank notification state

findings.body: The new routes are `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"`, and the controller action mutates `TopicUser#notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` unconditionally as soon as the request is handled (no separate 'confirm' click - the Ember page only reflects the state after the mutation already happened). Rails' `protect_from_forgery` (app/controllers/application_controller.rb:21) only protects non-GET verbs by default, so this GET action has no CSRF token check. This is a real, exploitable side effect on a safe HTTP method: a logged-in user's notification settings for an arbitrary topic can be changed just by their browser issuing a GET to this URL (e.g. via an `` on a third-party page, a link-prefetching browser feature, or an email/URL security scanner that pre-fetches links found in inbound mail - which is exactly the channel this URL is delivered through, since it's embedded in notification emails). Contrast with existing mutating topic actions in this controller (`star`, `mute`, `unmute`, `bookmark`, etc.) which are all exposed via `PUT`, not `GET`.
findings.title: Unsubscribe mutates state on a plain GET request with no CSRF protection or confirmation step

findings.body:
Every other mutation of `notification_level` in the codebase goes through `TopicUser.change`, which also stamps `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` and publishes a `MessageBus` `notification_level_change` event so other open tabs/sessions for the same user update live (see app/models/topic_user.rb `change`, `set_notifications_to_current_user`, and the tracking-scope-adjacent write paths that were all reformatted-but-unchanged in this diff). `TopicsController#unsubscribe` instead does a raw `find_by` + attribute assignment + `save!`, so:
- No MessageBus publish happens, so any other open browser tab for that user won't reflect the new notification level until reload.
- `notifications_reason_id`/`notifications_changed_at` are left stale/unset, which is inconsistent with how notification-level changes are recorded everywhere else and could confuse the `notificationReasonText` logic (topic-details.js.es6) that reads `notifications_reason_id`.
findings.title: unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change, losing MessageBus broadcast and audit fields

findings.body:
`TopicsController#show` redirects slug mismatches via `redirect_to_correct_topic`, which uses `topic.relative_url`, appends `.json` when `request.format.json?`, and preserves the `page` query param. The new `unsubscribe` action instead does:
```ruby
return redirect_to @topic_view.topic.unsubscribe_url, status: 301
```
where `unsubscribe_url` (`app/models/topic.rb`) is built from the absolute `url` (`Discourse.base_url` + slug + id + `/unsubscribe`) and never checks `request.format.json?`. Since `slugs_do_not_match` alone (regardless of format) triggers this branch, a JSON API request hit with a stale slug gets 301-redirected to a non-JSON HTML URL, unlike every other slug-correcting redirect in this controller.
findings.title: Slug-mismatch redirect in unsubscribe drops JSON format/query params, unlike the existing redirect helper

findings.body: TopicsController#unsubscribe does `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` and immediately calls `tu.notification_level`. `find_by` returns nil whenever the user has no TopicUser row for that topic yet (e.g. they were never emailed about it and never visited it, or the row was deleted). Because the route only requires the user to be logged in and able to see the topic (guardian check inside TopicView.new), any authenticated user can hit `GET /t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` for a topic they have no history with and trigger `undefined method 'notification_level' for nil:NilClass`, producing an unhandled 500 instead of muting the topic. Every other place in the codebase that mutates notification_level (TopicUser.change, used by set_notifications/toggle_mute) safely creates the row when it's missing; this new code path doesn't.
findings.title: Unsubscribe action crashes with NoMethodError when no TopicUser record exists

findings.body: The new action does `tu.notification_level = ...; tu.save!` directly instead of going through `TopicUser.change`, which is the convention used by every other notification-level mutation (set_notifications, toggle_mute, update_last_read, auto_track). As a result it skips: (1) the `MessageBus.publish("/topic/#{topic_id}", {notification_level_change: ...})` broadcast that keeps other open tabs/the topic-notifications-button in sync in real time, and (2) setting `notifications_reason_id`/`notifications_changed_at`, which the rest of the app relies on for reporting why/when a level changed.

findings.body: lib/email/message_builder.rb interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}` into the `unsubscribe_link` I18n string (config/locales/server.en.yml) whenever `@opts[:add_unsubscribe_link]` is true, in both `body` and `html_part`. `MessageBuilder#initialize` only defaults `site_name`, `base_url`, and `user_preferences_url` — `unsubscribe_url` has no default and no guard. Only `UserNotifications#send_notification_email` was updated to pass `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url`; any other caller of `build_email`/`MessageBuilder` (plugins, future core mailers) that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without also passing `unsubscribe_url` will hit a missing-interpolation-argument error and fail to send the email entirely, where previously it degraded gracefully (the old string only needed `user_preferences_url`, which was always present).
findings.title: MessageBuilder now requires callers to supply unsubscribe_url or email generation blows up

findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key (src/sentry/api/paginator.py, new code) does `int(math.floor(value) if self._is_asc(for_prev) else math.ceil(value))` directly on `getattr(item, self.key)`. This is the numeric variant lifted from `Paginator` (mirrors line 224 exactly). But the only caller, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, invokes it with `order_by="-datetime"` against `AuditLogEntry.datetime`, a DateTimeField. `math.floor(datetime_obj)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. `DateTimePaginator.get_item_key` (the class this was presumably meant to extend/reuse) first converts to a float timestamp before flooring/ceiling — that conversion is missing here. `build_cursor` calls `key(results[0])` unconditionally whenever there are results and no cursor value yet, so this crashes on literally the first page of any request that takes the optimized_pagination=true path and returns at least one row. This isn't an edge case — it's guaranteed to fail on normal use.
findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key is copied from the numeric Paginator, not DateTimePaginator — will TypeError on every real use

findings.body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` (negative). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly asserts against negative start/stop (`Negative indexing is not supported.`), raising AssertionError. `cursor.offset` comes straight from client-supplied `?cursor=value:offset:is_prev` via `Cursor.from_string` (src/sentry/utils/cursors.py:58-59), which does `int(bits[1])` with no range validation — any negative integer is accepted. `Endpoint.paginate` (src/sentry/api/base.py:525-541) only catches `BadPaginationError`; AssertionError propagates as an unhandled 500. So any request with `optimized_pagination=true&cursor=0:-1:0` reliably 500s. The comment above this code ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') is factually wrong.
findings.title: Negative-offset slicing on a Django QuerySet raises an unhandled AssertionError (500), and the input is fully attacker/user controlled

findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is presented in comments as restricting this to 'authorized administrators', but `has_global_access` is a boolean on OrganizationMember that defaults to True for any member not restricted to specific teams (src/sentry/models/organizationmember.py:216, confirmed by the comment in src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_member/team_details.py:169: 'access.has_global_access is True for all integration tokens'). This means essentially any ordinary org member (not just admins/superusers) can opt into the OptimizedCursorPaginator path via `?optimized_pagination=true`, which directly widens the reachable population for the P0 crashes above.
findings.title: Authorization gate for the 'advanced' path is not admin-only — has_global_access defaults to True for ordinary members

findings.body: `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is typed `RpcOrganizationMember | None = None` (src/sentry/organizations/services/organization/model.py:346). The new line `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` runs unconditionally on every GET to this endpoint (not gated by the optimized_pagination query param), regardless of whether the caller wants the new pagination behavior at all. If a non-superuser request reaches this endpoint with `organization_context.member` None — plausible for some auth paths since `OrganizationAuditPermission.has_object_permission` only requires org:write scope or active superuser, not necessarily an OrganizationMember record — this line raises AttributeError, breaking the endpoint entirely, including for callers who never asked for optimized pagination.
findings.title: organization_context.member can be None, causing an unconditional AttributeError before the feature flag is even checked

findings.body: The diff to `BasePaginator.get_result` (used by every subclass: Paginator, DateTimePaginator, etc. — not just the audit log endpoint) changes `stop = offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to clamp only when `not cursor.is_prev`: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. Two problems: (1) it silently coerces a client-supplied negative offset to 0 instead of surfacing a validation error, changing pagination semantics app-wide as an undocumented side effect of an 'audit logs' PR — this masks malformed/malicious cursors as a normal first page rather than failing loudly; (2) the fix is asymmetric — for `cursor.is_prev=True` the offset is left unclamped, so a negative offset on a 'previous page' cursor still hits Django's QuerySet negative-indexing assertion and crashes, exactly the failure mode the forward-path change was trying to avoid. This is broad-blast-radius, untested behavior change bundled into a feature-flagged endpoint change.
findings.title: Shared BasePaginator.get_result changed for every cursor-paginated endpoint in the codebase, with inconsistent and silent handling of negative offsets

findings.body: A comment claiming 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' was added directly above `self.offset = int(offset)`, but no validation or behavior actually changed at this call site — negative offsets were already unvalidated before this diff. The comment asserts a capability/rationale that isn't backed by any change here, and reads as the kind of narrative padding used to justify the unsafe negative-offset handling introduced elsewhere in this same change (see P0/P1 findings on paginator.py). Low functional impact on its own, but it's misleading and should be removed or corrected.

findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` runs unconditionally for every GET, before the `use_optimized` branch is even checked. When the request is authenticated via an org auth token (`OrgAuthTokenAuthentication`), `request.user` is `AnonymousUser` (src/sentry/api/authentication.py transform_auth passes user_id=None into `organization_service.get_organization_by_id`), so `organization_context.member` resolves to `None` (src/sentry/organizations/services/organization/impl.py get_organization_by_id skips the membership lookup when user_id is None, and `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is typed `Optional`). Such requests pass `OrganizationAuditPermission` via scope-based access (`org:write` from the token), so they legitimately reach this line and then crash with `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`. This is a regression versus the prior behavior, which never touched `organization_context.member` and always paginated successfully. Fix by guarding on `organization_context.member is not None` before accessing `.has_global_access`, and only evaluate `enable_advanced` when `use_optimized` is true.
findings.title: [P1] Audit log endpoint 500s for every org-token-authenticated request, regardless of optimized_pagination

findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` (paginator.py:838-840) is copied verbatim from the numeric `Paginator.get_item_key` (`int(math.floor(value) ... math.ceil(value))`) instead of `DateTimePaginator`'s datetime-aware version, which first converts via `value.strftime("%s.%f")`. The only caller (`organization_auditlogs.py`) instantiates this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value = getattr(item, "datetime")` is a `datetime.datetime` object; `math.floor`/`math.ceil` require `__floor__`/`__index__`, which `datetime` does not implement, so both raise `TypeError`. `build_cursor` (utils/cursors.py `_build_next_values`/`_build_prev_values`) calls `get_item_key` on the first/last result whenever the result set is non-empty — i.e. on the very first request with the default `Cursor(0,0,0)`, no crafted cursor needed. Separately, `value_from_cursor` (paginator.py:842-843) also mirrors the numeric `Paginator` and returns `cursor.value` unmodified instead of converting back to a `datetime` (as `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor` does); when a client supplies a non-zero cursor value, that raw number is bound as a SQL parameter against the `datetime` timestamp column in `build_queryset`'s `.extra(where=...)` clause, which Postgres rejects (`operator does not exist: timestamp with time zone >= integer`) since there's no implicit cast. Net effect: `optimized_pagination=true` is 100% non-functional for its only caller — it fails on the first request via the `get_item_key` path, and independently fails on any request carrying a client-supplied cursor value via the `value_from_cursor`/`build_queryset` path. The class needs `DateTimePaginator`'s conversion logic, not `Paginator`'s.
findings.title: [P1] OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on every non-empty result: reuses numeric key logic against a datetime column

findings.body: When `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` (negative). Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for any slice with a negative `start`, regardless of `stop` — it does not reinterpret the index Python-list-style from the end, contrary to the surrounding comments ("enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level"). Since `Cursor.from_string` parses the offset straight from the client-supplied cursor string with no lower-bound validation, an admin can trigger this by passing a manually crafted cursor (e.g. `cursor=<value>:-1:0`); the request will always fail with an unhandled `ValueError` (500) rather than performing the advertised bidirectional navigation. This is the core feature named in the PR description ("Enhanced cursor offset support for efficient bi-directional navigation") and it cannot work as written.
findings.title: [P2] Negative-offset "advanced pagination" branch is unconditionally broken: Django rejects negative queryset slices

findings.body: `enable_advanced` is gated on `request.user.is_superuser` (the persistent account flag), while the endpoint's own permission class, `OrganizationAuditPermission.has_object_permission` (api/bases/organization.py), only grants superuser access via `is_active_superuser(request)` — a session/mode-scoped check requiring explicit superuser-mode activation. A superuser account that is also an ordinary org member with `org:write` scope reaches this endpoint through the membership path (never evaluating `is_active_superuser`), and then trips `enable_advanced=True` purely because the account has the superuser bit set, independent of whether superuser mode was ever activated for the session. This diverges from the security boundary the rest of the codebase (and this endpoint's own permission class) enforces for privileged actions, and contradicts the comment's stated intent ("Enable advanced pagination features for authorized administrators"). Use `is_active_superuser(request)` for consistency.
findings.title: [P2] Advanced-pagination gate checks the static is_superuser flag, not active superuser mode

findings.body: In `BasePaginator.get_result`, `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes forward-pagination behavior: previously `queryset[offset:stop]` with a negative `offset` (e.g. a corrupted or manually crafted cursor) would raise Django's `ValueError` for any endpoint built on `BasePaginator`/`Paginator`/`DateTimePaginator` (this base class change is not opt-in). Now such a cursor is silently reinterpreted as offset 0 and returns the first page without any error, masking client-side cursor corruption or tampering rather than surfacing it. Low severity since no incorrect/unauthorized data is returned, but it's a silent behavior change across every paginator built on this base.
findings.title: [P3] Negative cursor offsets are now silently clamped to page 1 instead of surfacing an error

validation_gaps: No test was executed against a live Django/Postgres stack to directly reproduce the AttributeError, TypeError, ValueError, and Postgres operator-mismatch failures; conclusions are based on documented/well-known framework and language semantics (Django QuerySet negative-slice rejection, math.floor requiring __floor__, Postgres lacking implicit numeric-to-timestamp casts) rather than an executed repro in this environment.

The exact authentication classes enabled for OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint were traced via ControlSiloOrganizationEndpoint/DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION and OrgAuthTokenAuthentication, but this fixture does not include a runnable settings/URL config to empirically confirm org auth tokens are actually routed to this specific endpoint in production; the code path was confirmed structurally, not via a live request.
No tests were added by this commit for the new OptimizedCursorPaginator or the endpoint's new branch, so there is no existing automated check that would have caught F1/F2 before merge.

findings.body: organization_auditlogs.py gates the new 'advanced pagination' feature with `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, with a comment claiming this enables the feature 'for authorized administrators'. But `OrganizationMember.has_global_access` (src/sentry/models/organizationmember.py:216) is a legacy field meaning 'this member has access to all projects in the org' (see sentry/auth/access.py:204-208 docstring), unrelated to admin/superuser status, and it defaults to `True`. Any ordinary, non-admin organization member with this (commonly default) flag set can trivially enable the 'advanced' branch simply by passing `?optimized_pagination=true`, defeating the intended admin-only restriction entirely.
findings.title: Broken admin gate: has_global_access is not an authorization flag and defaults to True

findings.body: The new code checks raw `request.user.is_superuser` instead of the codebase's established `is_active_superuser(request)` pattern (imported from sentry.auth.superuser), which is used just a few lines away by `OrganizationAuditPermission.has_object_permission` in the same file's base class (src/sentry/api/bases/organization.py:110-124) specifically to require a freshly-elevated superuser session rather than the raw DB flag. Using the raw flag here reintroduces a security control regression that Sentry deliberately guards against elsewhere in this exact endpoint's permission chain.
findings.title: Superuser check bypasses Sentry's active-superuser session control

findings.body: `get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(value) if ... else math.ceil(value))` directly on `getattr(item, self.key)`. For this endpoint, `self.key` is `datetime` (from `order_by="-datetime"`), so `value` is a `datetime.datetime` instance. `math.floor`/`math.ceil` require a real number and raise `TypeError: type datetime.datetime doesn't define __floor__ method` for datetime objects. Contrast with the adjacent, correct `DateTimePaginator.get_item_key` (paginator.py:233-236) which first converts to a float timestamp via `value.strftime("%s.%f")`. Since `build_cursor` calls `get_item_key` on every result set to compute next/prev cursors, every single call to this endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` (from a superuser or, per the finding above, from almost any org member) will raise an unhandled TypeError and return a 500.
findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime fields (TypeError)

findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged. `get_item_key` (if it worked) encodes datetimes as `float(strftime(...)) * multiplier`-style integers, but there is no corresponding decode step (compare to `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor`, paginator.py:238-241, which does `datetime.fromtimestamp(float(cursor.value) / self.multiplier)`). On any subsequent page request, the raw integer cursor value would be passed into `build_queryset` and used as `datetime >= %s` / `datetime <= %s` SQL parameters against a timestamp column, which is a type mismatch that will error or silently produce incorrect filtering at the database layer even if the TypeError above were fixed.
findings.title: value_from_cursor does not decode the encoded cursor value back to a datetime

findings.body: When `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly asserts non-negative slice bounds ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so this path raises `AssertionError` rather than the 'efficient bidirectional pagination' described in the comments. The comment 'This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' / 'Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually incorrect — Django does the opposite (rejects it outright).
findings.title: Negative-offset 'advanced pagination' cannot function as described

findings.body: `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is documented as nullable ('member can be None when the given user_id does not have membership with the given organization'). The new code accesses `organization_context.member.has_global_access` without a None check. `request.user.is_superuser or ...` short-circuits in the common superuser case, but any code path where a caller passes the base permission check without `request.user.is_superuser` being True and without an org membership (e.g., future permission changes, or other callers of similar patterns) would raise an unhandled AttributeError.
findings.title: organization_context.member can be None, risking AttributeError

Given the class is broken on first use (see TypeError finding), a basic test exercising `optimized_pagination=true` against the audit log endpoint would have caught this before merge.

findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `start_offset = cursor.offset` (negative) and then `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative slice bounds and raises `AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.')` - it does not "properly handle negative slicing automatically" as the added comment claims. `Endpoint.paginate()` (src/sentry/api/base.py:525-541) only catches `BadPaginationError`, so this AssertionError propagates as an unhandled 500. Since `Cursor.from_string` (src/sentry/utils/cursors.py:53-61) parses the offset with a bare `int(bits[1])` with no sign validation, and `get_cursor`/`get_cursor_from_request` do no additional validation, any caller can trigger this by requesting `GET .../audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true&cursor=0:-1:0` while `enable_advanced` is true (any org:write-scoped member whose `OrganizationMember.has_global_access` is true, which is the DB default - see next finding). This means the entire feature this PR is meant to ship - "efficient bidirectional pagination"/negative-offset traversal - is dead code that always fails when actually exercised.
findings.title: [P1] OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch always crashes with an unhandled AssertionError

findings.body: `BasePaginator.get_result` (used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and every other subclass across the whole API, not only the new audit-log paginator) changed from `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset; results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. Previously an invalid/tampered forward cursor with a negative offset raised `AssertionError` (surfaced as a loud failure); now it is silently clamped to 0 and treated as a valid request for page one, with no error and no indication to the client that its cursor was invalid. This is an unscoped behavior change to shared, widely used infrastructure for a PR whose stated scope is audit-log pagination, it is asymmetric (the `is_prev` branch still passes a raw, possibly negative, offset straight through and will still crash), and no test in the diff exercises this new clamp or the asymmetry.
findings.title: [P2] Shared BasePaginator.get_result now silently masks negative cursor offsets across every cursor-paginated endpoint, not just audit logs

findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is commented as restricting the optimized path to "authorized administrators," but `OrganizationMember.has_global_access` (src/sentry/models/organizationmember.py:216) is a plain DB field that `default=True` for any member who is not explicitly restricted to specific teams - it signals "not team-restricted," not "is an admin." Because this endpoint already requires `org:write` scope via `OrganizationAuditPermission` (src/sentry/api/bases/organization.py:110-111), and members holding that scope are essentially never team-restricted, this second check adds no real restriction over what the endpoint's existing permission class already grants; it does not reduce the reachable population the comments imply it does.
findings.title: [P3] "authorized administrators" gate is effectively a no-op: has_global_access defaults to true for the members who already pass the existing permission check

validation_gaps: Could not execute the negative-offset code path against a live Django/Postgres instance in this environment (no Django installation present in the fixture) to directly reproduce the AssertionError; the conclusion relies on Django's long-standing, documented QuerySet slicing contract rather than an executed repro.

Did not verify at runtime whether any WSGI/DRF exception-handling middleware in this deployment converts the AssertionError to something other than a 500 (e.g., custom error pages); assessed from the exception handling visible in Endpoint.paginate and standard DRF/Django behavior only.
Did not enumerate real organizations' has_global_access distribution; the P3 finding is based on the field's default value and role semantics in code, not measured production data.
